h1: The 8 Best 5-Port Network Switches of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight 5-port network switches, from plain gigabit boxes to PoE, 2.5G and 10G models, with clear picks by budget.
summary: The TP-Link TL-SG105 is the best 5-port switch for most buyers: five gigabit ports, QoS, a metal case and a three-year warranty. The NETGEAR GS305 is the silent pick, and the TL-SG1005P is the best PoE option with a 65W budget. Pick the TL-SG105S-M2 for 2.5G and the TL-SX105 for 10G.
intro: Port count is the least useful number on a five-port switch. Two boxes with five identical sockets can differ by a factor of ten in speed, and one may quietly power your cameras over the cable while the other will not. Decide what each port needs to do before you compare any model, and the shortlist shrinks fast.

We reviewed eight unmanaged five-port switches on paper, using the spec lines for port speed, PoE budget, cooling, mounting and warranty. We ranked them for general home and small-office use, then spread out the PoE and multi-gig models so a reader with cameras, a NAS or a 2.5G router can jump straight to the one that matches their gear instead of reading past it. Where a listing is silent on a spec such as warranty, we treat that as unknown.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: The safe default for turning one wall jack into five gigabit ports.
products.description:
The TP-Link TL-SG105 has five gigabit ports, QoS and IGMP snooping, a metal case that mounts on a desk or wall, and a three-year warranty, in the under $25 bucket. QoS prioritizes traffic so a video call survives a download, and IGMP snooping keeps multicast traffic from flooding every port.

It ranks first because it adds those traffic features and a longer warranty to the same gigabit speed the NETGEAR GS305 offers. Compared with the GS105NA, it costs less. The multi-gig models beat it on speed but cost more and pay off only with matching gear.

Buy it for a desk, TV or console setup that needs more wired ports. The caveat is simple: it is gigabit only with no PoE, so skip it if your internet is faster than gigabit.
products.idealFor: Anyone adding wired ports for a desk, TV or console setup.
products.skipIf: You have multi-gig internet or need to power devices over the cable.

products.name: NETGEAR GS305 5-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: A silent, energy-aware gigabit switch for bedrooms and quiet desks.
products.description:
The NETGEAR GS305 has five gigabit ports, a fanless design, 802.3az energy-efficient Ethernet and desktop or wall mounting, in the under $25 bucket. Without a fan it makes no noise at all, and 802.3az lowers power draw when a link is idle.

It ranks second because it lists no QoS, so the TL-SG105 edges it for busy shared networks. It wins for a quiet room, though, and it costs the same.

Buy it for a bedroom or living room where silence matters more than traffic shaping. Skip it if you want prioritization features on the box. A fanless case cools itself through the metal, so leave the vents clear and avoid burying it under cables.
products.idealFor: Bedroom, living-room or quiet desk setups.
products.skipIf: You want traffic prioritisation features on the box.

products.name: NETGEAR GS105NA 5-Port Gigabit Switch
products.verdict: Plain gigabit with the strongest warranty promise in the group.
products.description:
The NETGEAR GS105NA is a five-port gigabit switch with a fanless design, desktop or wall mounting and the NETGEAR Lifetime Warranty, in the $25 to $50 bucket. A lifetime promise is rare on networking gear and suits a switch you want to forget in a cabinet.

It ranks third because it costs more than the GS305 for the same ports, and it lists no extra traffic features. The warranty is what you pay for, and it is the strongest in the group.

Buy it for a closet or cabinet install that will run for years. Skip it if you want the lowest price. Compare it with the TL-SG105, which carries a three-year warranty and QoS, before paying the premium for the lifetime term.
products.idealFor: Set-and-forget installs in cabinets and closets.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest price or extra traffic features.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 5-Port 2.5G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: The affordable step up when your internet is faster than gigabit.
products.description:
The TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 has five 2.5G ports, 25Gbps switching capacity, a compact metal case and works over existing Cat5e cable. That last point matters: you can upgrade to 2.5G without rewiring the house, since Cat5e handles it for typical runs.

It ranks fourth since the speed helps only when something on your network is faster than gigabit. A router or NAS with a 2.5G port is the case where it pays off, and it costs only a little more than the NETGEAR GS105NA.

Buy it if you have 2.5G gear to connect. Skip it if your whole network is gigabit, because the TL-SG105 does the job for less. It has no PoE, so cameras will need their own power.
products.idealFor: Homes with 2.5G routers, NAS boxes or desktops.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SX105 5-Port 10G Unmanaged Switch
products.verdict: Full 10G on every port for workstations and fast storage.
products.description:
The TP-Link TL-SX105 has five 10G ports, 100Gbps switching capacity and auto-negotiation from 100Mb through 10G, in a fanless case with a three-year warranty. Ten gigabit on every port means workstations and a NAS can move large files at the speed of the link.

It ranks fifth because it is the most expensive switch here, and most homes have no 10G devices to connect. It stands apart from the 2.5G model by giving you headroom for a future NAS.

Buy it if you edit video from shared storage or run a fast server. Skip it if you have no 10G gear. Because it auto-negotiates down, older devices still work, so it can serve as a long-term backbone.
products.idealFor: Workstations and NAS setups that need 10G.
products.skipIf: You have no 10G devices to plug in.

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG1005P 5-Port Gigabit PoE Switch
products.verdict: Powers four devices over the cable with a clear 65W budget.
products.description:
The TP-Link TL-SG1005P has four PoE+ ports with a 65W total budget, one uplink, QoS, IGMP snooping and a three-year warranty. Power over Ethernet sends electricity down the same cable as data, so a camera or access point needs no wall adapter.

It ranks sixth because PoE helps only if you own PoE gear, and the 65W is shared across all four ports, not 65W each. The NETGEAR GS305P has a slightly smaller 63W budget but smarter reallocation.

Buy it for a small camera or access point install. Skip it if you have no PoE devices. Add up the wattage of your devices first, since a few cameras plus an access point can exhaust 65W quickly.
products.idealFor: Small camera or access point installs.

products.name: NETGEAR GS305P 5-Port PoE Gigabit Switch
products.verdict: A fanless PoE switch that reallocates power between ports.
products.description:
The NETGEAR GS305P has four PoE+ ports sharing 63W, dynamic PoE power reallocation, a fanless unmanaged design and plug and play setup. Dynamic reallocation hands unused wattage from a quiet port to a busy one, which stretches a small budget across a mixed set of devices.

It ranks seventh because the 63W budget is slightly smaller than the TL-SG1005P's 65W and no warranty term is listed. The listing's silence on the warranty is a minor gap.

Buy it for a quiet room with a mix of PoE devices. Skip it if you want the biggest PoE budget at this size. Fanless cooling means silence, but check that the case has room to breathe.
products.idealFor: Quiet rooms with a mix of PoE devices.
products.skipIf: You want the biggest PoE budget at this size.

products.name: TP-Link LS1005G Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Switch
products.verdict: A tiny, fanless budget switch for travel or tight spots.
products.description:
The TP-Link LS1005G Litewave has five ports, one uplink and four outputs, measures 2.8 x 3.5 x 0.9 inches and weighs 2.8 oz, fanless, in the under $25 bucket. It fits in a bag or behind a monitor, which no other switch here does.

It ranks last because it lists fewer features, with no QoS and no long warranty, and it offers no PoE. Its role is convenience, not performance.

Buy it for tight desks, travel bags and hidden installs. Skip it if you want QoS features or a long warranty. Small switches run quietly, but check the port layout against your cable lengths before ordering.
products.idealFor: Tight desks, travel bags and hidden installs.
products.skipIf: You want QoS features or a long warranty.

methodology.title: Port speed
methodology.description: We checked whether each switch runs gigabit, 2.5G or 10G on its ports, since that sets the ceiling for every device behind it.

methodology.title: PoE capability
methodology.description: We noted whether PoE is offered and how large the shared power budget is, because that limits how many devices can be powered.

methodology.title: Cooling and noise
methodology.description: We favoured fanless designs, as a switch often sits in a bedroom or on a desk.

methodology.title: Mounting and size
methodology.description: We looked at desktop and wall mounting options and overall footprint for small spaces.

methodology.title: Warranty and extras
methodology.description: We compared warranty terms and listed features such as QoS, IGMP snooping and energy efficiency.

whatMatters.detail: Port speed is how fast each socket can move data, usually 1G, 2.5G or 10G. It matters because a fast router or NAS is held back by a slower switch between them. Check the speed printed next to the port count in the product title, not just the word gigabit in a bullet, and confirm every port matches.

Power over Ethernet sends electricity down the same cable that carries data, which is how cameras and access points run without a wall adapter. The budget is a total shared across all PoE ports, so 65W does not mean 65W each. Add up the wattage of your devices and compare it with the listed total before you buy.

A fanless switch cools through its case, so it makes no sound at all. That matters if the switch lives in a bedroom or beside your desk. Look for the word fanless in the feature list, since a missing mention usually means the spec sheet does not promise it. Leave air around the case either way.

Some switches include wall-mount slots, which frees desk space and keeps cables tidy. It matters most in small rooms and cabinets. Check the listing for the words wall mount and look at the dimensions to be sure it fits your spot. The TL-SG105 and NETGEAR models allow it, while the LS1005G is tiny.

A longer warranty protects a switch that will run around the clock for years. QoS and IGMP snooping help when streaming and calls share the line. Read the bullet points for a warranty term, and treat a missing term as unknown rather than as good news. NETGEAR's GS105NA lists lifetime coverage.

howToChoose.intro: Match the switch to the fastest device it will serve.

cards.label: Plain switch
cards.text: Moves data only, and devices need their own power adapters. The TP-Link TL-SG105, NETGEAR GS305, NETGEAR GS105NA and TP-Link LS1005G fall here.

cards.label: PoE switch
cards.text: Carries power and data on one cable, so cameras and access points need no wall plug. The TP-Link TL-SG1005P and NETGEAR GS305P do this with a shared budget of about 63W to 65W.

howToChoose.note: Most buyers should pick a plain switch unless a specific device needs PoE.

rows: Metal case for a desk or wall

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: PoE+ ports and a total budget that covers every camera's wattage with some spare.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The TP-Link TL-SG1005P lists 65W across four ports, and the NETGEAR GS305P lists 63W with dynamic reallocation.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You own a 2.5G router or a NAS, in which case the TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 or TP-Link TL-SX105 stops the switch being the bottleneck.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Everything is gigabit, where the TP-Link TL-SG105 or NETGEAR GS305 does the whole job.

faq.q: Will a 5-port switch slow down my internet?
faq.a: Not if its ports are at least as fast as your connection. A gigabit switch can cap a faster plan, so match the switch speed to your fastest device. The TL-SG105S-M2 handles 2.5G internet, and the TL-SX105 handles 10G.

faq.q: Do I need a managed switch?
faq.a: These are unmanaged, meaning you plug them in and they work. That is enough for most homes and small offices, including the TL-SG105 and GS305. Only buy managed if you need VLANs or per-port controls, which none of the picks here provide.

faq.q: Is the TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 worth it over the TL-SG105?
faq.a: Only if you have a 2.5G router, NAS or computer to use the extra speed. Otherwise the gigabit TL-SG105 does the same job for less, and its three-year warranty is comparable.

faq.q: How do I set up a PoE switch?
faq.a: Plug the uplink into your router, then connect each PoE device directly. Check that the combined wattage of your devices fits the total budget, such as 65W on the TL-SG1005P or 63W on the NETGEAR GS305P.

No software updates are needed on an unmanaged switch. Keep the vents clear and dust it occasionally, especially fanless models like the GS305 that cool through the case, and avoid stacking gear on top.

faq.q: Can I use the 10G switch with older gear?
faq.a: Yes, the TL-SX105 lists auto-negotiation from 100Mb up to 10G, so older devices still connect at their own speed. Only 10G devices use the full speed of the link, so a mixed network works fine.

finalTake: The TP-Link TL-SG105 is the right five-port switch for most people: five gigabit ports, QoS and a solid warranty for very little money. Choose the NETGEAR GS305 for silence and the TL-SG1005P if cameras need power. Buy 2.5G or 10G only when your devices can use it. Match the speed to your fastest device first.
